note: Committed headline findings for the dashboard Overview. Every value carries a `source` citing the committed artifact it traces to. Numbers are the honest research record; nothing here is a profitability claim.

plain_story.headline: We tested 38 ways to beat this market. After fees, none survived.
paragraphs: Kalshi runs a market on a simple bet: will Bitcoin be higher 15 minutes from now? Traders buy and sell "yes" and "no", and the price is the crowd's live estimate of the probability.

This lab asked, rigorously, whether any model or trading rule can do better than that crowd price. Across 38 separate ideas — machine-learning models, stale-quote sniping, market-making, cross-coin signals — the answer was the same: the market's own price is already the best forecaster, and once you subtract trading costs (about 2.5 cents a round trip), every strategy loses.

One pattern did slip through the statistical filters, but a close look showed it is a trap: it wins tiny amounts almost every time while risking a rare, huge loss. So the honest score is 38 tested, 1 survivor, 0 you would actually trade. That negative result — measured carefully enough to trust — is the point.

tiles.label: Market-implied window-ECE
tiles.plain: How close is the market price to reality?
tiles.caption: The market's own price is the best-calibrated forecaster we measured — its stated odds are almost exactly right.
tiles.explain: ECE (calibration error) is the average gap between a predicted probability and how often it actually happens. Lower is better; 0.020 means the price is off by about 2 points on average.

tiles.label: Best model window-ECE
tiles.plain: Can our best model do better?
tiles.caption: No. Every model we trained is worse-calibrated than the market price it was trying to beat.
tiles.explain: Same calibration-error yardstick as the tile on the left — higher (worse) here than the market's 0.020.

tiles.label: Hypotheses tested
tiles.plain: How many ways did we try to win?
tiles.caption: 38 distinct trading ideas, each tested honestly and written up. The full record is the Research Map.
tiles.explain: Each "leg" is one hypothesis with a method, a key number, and a verdict.

tiles.label: Round-trip cost
tiles.caption: About 2.5 cents per round trip (~1c spread + ~1.5c fee). No taker strategy earned enough to clear it.
tiles.explain: The spread is the gap between buy and sell prices; the fee is Kalshi's cut. A strategy has to beat both just to break even.

tiles.label: Survived the gauntlet
tiles.caption: One cell passed every statistical filter (including a locked-away holdout it had never seen) — the deep-favorite maker trade.
tiles.explain: The "gauntlet" adjusts for how many ideas were tried, so a lucky-looking result can't sneak through. Surviving it is rare and meaningful.

tiles.label: Actually tradeable
tiles.caption: No. The survivor collects ~2–4c almost every time but risks a −96c loss when it's wrong — a penny in front of a steamroller.
tiles.explain: The statistical score can't see that rare huge loss because it never showed up in the small winning sample. That blind spot is exactly why it isn't bankable.

fees_kill_alpha.headline: Fees kill the alpha
fees_kill_alpha.plain: Even models that look smart before costs turn into losers after the spread and fee are subtracted.
fees_kill_alpha.detail: On the committed 95-window sample, the executable backtest (buying at the real ask price, then subtracting fees) turns every trained model net-negative. The market-implied forecaster never trades — it has no edge over itself.

verdict_of_the_lab: The 15-minute Bitcoin market on Kalshi is efficient after costs at retail speed: the crowd price already reflects everything our whole feature library knows. The honest negative result is the product.

glossary.ECE: Calibration error — the average gap between a predicted probability and how often it really happens. Lower is better.
glossary.calibration: How well stated odds match reality. A well-calibrated 70% forecast is right about 70% of the time.
glossary.market-implied: The probability implied by the live market price — the crowd's own forecast.
glossary.reliability diagram: A chart that plots predicted probability against what actually happened. A perfect forecaster sits on the diagonal line.
glossary.executable backtest: A replay that fills trades at the real price you could have gotten (the ask), then subtracts fees — not an optimistic mid-price.
glossary.taker: A trader who crosses the spread to trade immediately, paying the fee.
glossary.maker: A trader who posts a resting order and waits to be filled, hoping to avoid the spread.
glossary.spread: The gap between the best buy price and best sell price.
glossary.Deflated Sharpe Ratio: A performance score adjusted for how many strategies were tried — it deflates results that only look good because you searched a lot.
glossary.DSR: Deflated Sharpe Ratio — a performance score adjusted for how many strategies were tried.
glossary.PBO: Probability of Backtest Overfitting — the chance a strategy's edge is just curve-fitting that won't repeat.
glossary.sealed holdout: A slice of data locked away and tested against exactly once, so a strategy can't be tuned to it.
glossary.profit factor: Gross wins divided by gross losses. Above 1 makes money; around 1 is break-even.
glossary.reprice-lag: The idea that Kalshi's price is slow to update after Bitcoin moves, leaving a brief stale quote to pick off.
